title: Navigating the maze: Deepfakes, cognitive ability, and social media news skepticism
screen_reason: US online survey (Qualtrics panel, February 2020). Although the paper's aim is to predict social media news skepticism, the Measures section reports one descriptive share of respondents with a denominator: 39.1% said yes to ever having inadvertently shared a deepfake. That is a self-reported SHARING share (RECALL, recall_subtype sharing) and qualifies under the 'aim is something else but a descriptive share is reported' rule.

estimates.platform: Not specified; the item asks about sharing a deepfake, with no platform named (the companion exposure items covered social media sites and the Internet other than social media)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they ever shared a deepfake without realizing it was fake
estimates.denominator: 764 US adult respondents from a Qualtrics online national panel who were aware of deepfakes before the survey (61.4% of the 1,244 collected)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered yes to having 'ever shared a deepfake without realizing that it was fake and that you later found out that it was made up'
estimates.misinfo_def: Deepfakes use machine-learning algorithms to create video and audio of real people doing and saying untrue things
estimates.source_quote: Inadvertent deepfakes sharing (39.1% said yes, 1=yes, 0=no) was measured based on an item asking the participants if they had “ever shared a deepfake without realizing that it was fake and that you later found out that it was made up.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own retrospective judgement, anchored on later finding out the video was made up; no external verification of any shared item
estimates.moderator_quote: Keeping with the focus of this study, the rest of the analysis focuses only on respondents who were familiar with deepfakes prior to the survey. A total of 764 respondents (61.4%) were aware of deepfakes and formed the primary dataset for this study.
estimates.notes: The denominator is the deepfake-aware subsample, not the full panel: 39.1% is conditional on prior awareness of deepfakes, so it is not a population-wide sharing rate (the corresponding full-sample figure, N=1,244, is not given in the text; only replicated regression results are said to appear in the online appendix). Topic coded 'other' because the sharing item places no topical restriction on the deepfake; the paper's concern index separates deepfakes 'in general' from 'political deepfakes', but the sharing and exposure items are general. Regression tables use N=762 (two cases lost to listwise deletion); the 39.1% is reported against N=764.

missed_or_uncertain: Considered and not extracted: (1) 'A total of 764 respondents (61.4%) were aware of deepfakes' — awareness of the deepfake phenomenon before the survey, not encountering or being exposed to a deepfake, so not a RECALL-exposure estimate. (2) Deepfakes exposure (M=2.79; SD=1.43), an index of two 1-5 'how frequently do you come across deepfakes' items — a scale mean only, with no share of respondents above any threshold and no share reporting any, so no row per the scale-means exclusion. (3) Deepfakes concern (M=3.62; SD=1.20) and social media news skepticism (M=5.45; SD=1.24) — attitudes, not exposure or sharing shares. (4) Sample descriptors (57% males, 82% Whites) are demographics, not misinformation estimates. (5) '58.79% of the sample' below cognitive ability 6.10 and '41.21%' above — a moderator split, not a misinformation share. No behavioural or content data appear anywhere in the paper.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey, non-probability Qualtrics US national panel quota-matched to population age and gender distributions, fielded February 2020; 1,244 responses collected, analysis restricted to the 764 (61.4%) who reported prior awareness of deepfakes; regressions N=762. No response rate reported. All misinformation measures are single-item or two-item self-reports; inadvertent sharing is a single binary item with no reliability statistic (the two-item exposure and concern indices report Spearman-Brown coefficients of .92 and .91). No external coding or verification of any content, so no inter-rater reliability applies. Authors list self-report as a limitation.
rob.item6_quote: Inadvertent deepfakes sharing (39.1% said yes, 1=yes, 0=no) was measured based on an item asking the participants if they had “ever shared a deepfake without realizing that it was fake and that you later found out that it was made up.
rob.item10_quote: The total collected sample comprised 1244 responses, which were then filtered for individuals who were aware of deepfakes. The participants were provided with a definition of deepfakes and asked whether they were aware of deepfakes before the survey (Supplemental Appendix A1). Keeping with the focus of this study, the rest of the analysis focuses only on respondents who were familiar with deepfakes prior to the survey. A total of 764 respondents (61.4%) were aware of deepfakes and formed the primary dataset for this study.
